q-83641:
The expected value of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot f(x).
$$

We're given the frequencies of the cracked eggs, so we can start by computing the corresponding probabilities. The total number of cartons is $10+7+2+1=20,$ so the corresponding probabilities are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(N=0)=f(0) & =\frac{10}{20}=\frac{1}{2} \\ P(N=1)=f(1) & =\frac{7}{20} \\ P(N=2)=f(2) & =\frac{2}{20}=\frac{1}{10} \\ P(N=3)=f(3) & =\frac{1}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

We organize these results in the table below.

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{7}{20}$ | $\frac{1}{10}$ | $\frac{1}{20}$ |

Now, summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[N] & =0\cdot f(0)+1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3) \\  & =0(\frac{1}{2})+1(\frac{7}{20})+2(\frac{1}{10})+3(\frac{1}{20}) \\  & =0+\frac{7}{20}+\frac{2}{10}+\frac{3}{20} \\  & =\frac{7}{20}+\frac{4}{20}+\frac{3}{20} \\  & =\frac{7+4+3}{20} \\  & =\frac{14}{20} \\  & =\frac{7}{10} \\  & =0.7.\end{aligned}
$$

q-79697:
A first order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)\,,
$$

where $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ do not depend on $y.$

$$

$$

We have

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+y}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}(\frac{x+y}{x}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x(x+y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2}+xy \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,+{{(-x)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}y & ={{{x}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-xy & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=-x$ and $Q(x)={x}^{2}.$

q-16400:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =1-4y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}y & ={{\frac{1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $Q(x)=\frac{1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}.$

q-103567:
To determine which of the following differential equations is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation, we attempt to write each option in the standard form.

A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Let's attempt to write $\frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-x{e}^{2x}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{y}$ in the standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-x{e}^{2x} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-x{e}^{2x}y & =y\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-x{e}^{2x}y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is in standard form with  $P(x)=-x{e}^{2x}$ and $Q(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Since the equation is written in standard form, we conclude that it is a first-order linear ODE.

All of the other equations cannot be written in the standard form, and therefore they are not first-order linear ODEs.

q-106744:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

If $v$ is an eigenvector, then there must exist a real number $\lambda $ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ Hence, we have

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=\lambda [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

This leads to the following system of equations for $\lambda :$

$$
{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda  \\ -2=-\lambda \end{aligned}
$$

This system has no solution. Therefore, $v$ is not an eigenvector of $A.$

Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}11 & -6 \\ -12 & 25\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}c+1 \\ c\end{aligned}] & =7[\begin{aligned}c+1 \\ c\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5c+11 \\ 13c-12\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}7c+7 \\ 7c\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

q-75611:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\lambda v \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 20-4k & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =(2k+1)[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}7 \\ 26-4k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2k+1 \\ 4k+2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}7=2k+1, \\ 26-4k=4k+2\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get

$$
7=2k+1\,⟹\,k=3.
$$

Now, substituting $k=3$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}26-4k & =4k+2 \\ 26-4\cdot 3 & =4\cdot 3+2 \\ 14 & =14,\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=3.$

q-75730:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. By the definition of an eigenvector, we have 

$$
Av=\frac{1}{4}v.
$$

 
Multiplying it by ${A}^{-1}$ from the left, we obtain 

$$
v=\frac{1}{4}{A}^{-1}v.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $4$, we get 

$$
{A}^{-1}v=4v.
$$

 
So, $v$ is an eigenvector  of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $4.$

**Note:** In general, an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\frac{1}{\lambda }.$

- Statement II is true. According to the statement above, an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =\frac{1}{-1}=-1.$

- Statement III is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(-v)=-Av=-(5v)=5(-v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(-v)=5(-v),$ and $-v\ne 0,$ this implies that $-v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =5.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

To find the complex conjugate of a vector, we take the complex conjugate of the entries of the vector. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\overset{―}{x}}_{2} & =\overset{―}{[\begin{aligned}-6\text{i} \\ 1+2\text{i}\end{aligned}]} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{-6\text{i}} \\ \overset{―}{1+2\text{i}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6\text{i} \\ 1-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the second vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{i}\cdot {\overset{―}{x}}_{2} & =\text{i}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6\text{i} \\ 1-2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6{\text{i}}^{2} \\ \text{i}-2{\text{i}}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2+\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+\text{i}\cdot {\overset{―}{x}}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}3-8\text{i} \\ -4+2\text{i}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3-8\text{i} \\ -2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
